pharm: Provides vitamin K1 needed for hepatic synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X; reverses vitamin K deficiency and the effect of vitamin K antagonist anticoagulants.
tags: BOXED WARNING: severe reactions with IV/IM use
quick: Anticoagulant-induced hypoprothrombinemia: 2.5-10 mg (up to 25 mg); newborn HDN prophylaxis: 0.5-1 mg IM once
Parenteral; oral forms absorbed better with fat-containing food
Former category C; use only if clearly needed (also used at delivery for the newborn)
Unknown if excreted in human milk; use with caution
Repeated large doses not warranted in liver disease if initial response is poor
summary: Phytomenadione (phytonadione, vitamin K1) is used for coagulation disorders due to faulty formation of factors II, VII, IX, and X caused by vitamin K deficiency or interference with vitamin K activity - including warfarin/coumarin-induced hypoprothrombinemia, hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, and hypoprothrombinemia from antibacterials, malabsorption (e.g., obstructive jaundice, biliary fistula, sprue, cystic fibrosis), or salicylates. The injectable emulsion carries a BOXED WARNING: severe reactions, including fatal anaphylactoid reactions, shock, and cardiac/respiratory arrest, have occurred during and immediately after intravenous and intramuscular injection, even with dilution and slow infusion - so the IV/IM routes should be reserved for when subcutaneous administration is not feasible. The subcutaneous route is preferred; when IV is unavoidable, inject very slowly (not exceeding 1 mg/min). It does not act immediately - measurable improvement in prothrombin time takes 1-2 hours.
indications: Anticoagulant-induced prothrombin deficiency caused by coumarin or indanedione derivatives
Prophylaxis and therapy of hemorrhagic disease of the newborn

Hypoprothrombinemia secondary to factors limiting absorption or synthesis of vitamin K (e.g., obstructive jaundice, biliary fistula, sprue, ulcerative colitis, celiac disease, intestinal resection, cystic fibrosis, regional enteritis)
Other drug-induced hypoprothrombinemia clearly due to interference with vitamin K metabolism (e.g., salicylates)

dosage.d: 2.5 to 10 mg initially (up to 25 mg, rarely 50 mg); repeat based on prothrombin time response
dosage.n: Prefer SC route; if IV is unavoidable, give very slowly, <=1 mg/min

dosage.c: Prophylaxis of hemorrhagic disease of the newborn
dosage.d: 0.5 to 1 mg as a single intramuscular dose within one hour of birth
dosage.n: Recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics

dosage.c: Treatment of hemorrhagic disease of the newborn
dosage.d: 1 mg subcutaneously or intramuscularly (higher doses if the mother received an oral anticoagulant)
dosage.n: Confirm with coagulation testing; blood/component therapy if bleeding is severe

admin: Whenever possible, give by the subcutaneous route (see boxed warning)
When IV is unavoidable, inject very slowly, not exceeding 1 mg per minute
Protect from light at all times; inspect for particulate matter and discoloration before use
Dilute only with preservative-free 0.9% sodium chloride, 5% dextrose, or 5% dextrose/sodium chloride; start administration immediately and discard unused diluted drug
Do not expect an immediate effect - allow 1-2 hours for measurable PT improvement; use blood/component therapy if bleeding is severe
moa: Phytomenadione is vitamin K1, required as a cofactor for the hepatic gamma-carboxylation that produces functional clotting factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, and X. By supplying vitamin K, it corrects deficiency states and overcomes the inhibition of vitamin K-dependent factor synthesis produced by coumarin/indanedione anticoagulants. It does not act immediately (synthesis of new factors takes time) and does not counteract heparin.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to phytonadione or any component of the formulation
relative: Intravenous or intramuscular route when subcutaneous is feasible (risk of severe reactions)
Use in patients who still require anticoagulation (over-correction restores thromboembolic risk)
Liver disease unresponsive to initial vitamin K (avoid repeated large doses)
monitor: Signs of anaphylactoid reaction during/after IV or IM injection

preg: Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted and it is not known whether phytonadione can cause fetal harm; it was formerly Pregnancy Category C. Give to a pregnant woman only if clearly needed. (It is also administered to the newborn at delivery.)
lact: It is not known whether phytonadione is excreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in milk, exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is defined in the labeling.
hepatic: Repeated large doses of vitamin K are not warranted in liver disease if the response to initial use is unsatisfactory - failure to respond may indicate the condition is inherently unresponsive to vitamin K.

major: Coumarin/indanedione anticoagulants (warfarin) - phytonadione antagonizes their effect; over-correction can produce temporary anticoagulant resistance and restore thrombotic risk
moderate: Heparin - phytonadione does NOT counteract the anticoagulant action of heparin
Broad-spectrum antibacterials and salicylates - may induce the hypoprothrombinemia that vitamin K treats
interactions.food: Oral absorption of vitamin K depends on bile and dietary fat (impaired in malabsorption/cholestasis).
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction described in the label.
interactions.diagnostics: Corrects prothrombin time/INR (the intended therapeutic monitoring parameter).

serious: Anaphylactoid / hypersensitivity reaction (shock, cardiac/respiratory arrest) with IV or IM use
Hyperbilirubinemia in the newborn (mainly with doses above recommended)
rare: Erythematous, indurated, pruritic plaques (sometimes scleroderma-like, persisting long-term) after repeated injection
emergency: Anaphylaxis / cardiovascular collapse during or immediately after IV/IM injection

monitoring: Prothrombin time / INR and coagulation response
Close observation during and after IV/IM administration for hypersensitivity
counsel: This vitamin K medicine reverses the effect of warfarin-type blood thinners and treats clotting problems from vitamin K deficiency
It does not work instantly - it can take 1-2 hours for blood tests to improve
An injection (especially into a vein or muscle) can rarely cause a serious allergic reaction, so it is usually given under the skin and with monitoring
Keep your prothrombin time/INR blood tests as scheduled
Tell your doctor about all blood thinners and other medicines you take
pk: Measurable PT improvement in 1-2 hours (no immediate coagulant effect)
Short; rapidly metabolized in the liver
Effect persists while newly synthesized clotting factors circulate
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light; keep ampules in carton until use
pearls: BOXED WARNING: severe, sometimes fatal anaphylactoid reactions with IV and IM use - prefer the subcutaneous route; if IV is unavoidable, give <=1 mg/min
Does NOT reverse heparin - only vitamin K antagonists (warfarin/coumarins)
Standard neonatal prophylaxis: 0.5-1 mg IM once within one hour of birth to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn (vitamin K deficiency bleeding)
Effect is delayed (1-2 hours for PT) - use fresh frozen plasma/factor concentrate for serious active bleeding
Over-correction in a patient who still needs anticoagulation can cause temporary warfarin resistance and re-expose them to clotting risk
missed: This medicine is usually given as needed by a healthcare professional based on coagulation tests rather than on a fixed schedule. If an oral dose for deficiency is missed, take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose; do not double up.
overdose: Excessive doses can cause over-correction of anticoagulation, producing temporary resistance to warfarin-type drugs and restoring thromboembolic risk; in newborns, doses above those recommended can cause hyperbilirubinemia. Manage supportively and adjust subsequent anticoagulation; for re-anticoagulation, larger doses of the vitamin K antagonist or a heparin (which acts by a different mechanism) may be needed.
